cim: Rise of artificial intelligence in Athens affects local artists
cim_eredeti: Rise of artificial intelligence in Athens affects local artists
szoveg_eredeti:
Over the past year, the rise of artificial intelligence has become more prominent in Athens. The increased use of AI-generated media by local businesses and student organizations concerns local artists.

Sam Boyde, a senior studying studio art, said he is as anti-AI as a person can be. Boyde said he feels a loss of hope seeing food trucks around campus using entirely AI-generated artwork.

“It looked horrible,” Boyd said. “It had a bunch of AI garbage on it, and it was actively unappetizing, And that makes even less sense to me because they're making that product. It seems like they could have just taken a picture of it and put it on the side of their truck.”

With so many artists in Athens, many suggest reaching out to students for quality artwork instead of using AI-generated media.

Reagan Nutter, a sophomore studying graphic design and visual communications, works for Vivid, a creative multimedia agency on campus. Nutter said Vivid offers to do pro bono work for local businesses to provide portfolio building materials for students.

“I think that AI is such a good asset, and I use it to help me with my own designs,” Nutter said. “There’s a very ethical and very smart way to use it. My one gripe that I have is as someone that wants to build a portfolio and get experience, seeing so many fully AI-generated posters, flyers, billboards. I would do that for free.”

For graphic designers like Nutter, AI can be a helpful tool when removing backgrounds and smaller tedious jobs. Artist Jacob Gardner agreed AI can be a tool for creatives to use.

“I really had to play around with it to just to begin to understand how interesting it can be, and I found ways for it to be very helpful without necessarily taking anything away from my personal touch,” Gardner said.

The views on using AI vary between artists, while some believe it can be used as a tool, others find that it doesn’t count as art when using AI. Claire Drayer, a sophomore studying graphic design, said she has always enjoyed creating art and it influenced her choice in major.

“I don't really consider it art because it's not something that you personally made, it's the same with writing something with AI or doing anything similar to that,” Drayer said. “It's not really a handmade thing, and that's what a lot of art is. It's creativity and using your brain to come up with ideas, and using your imagination, which really isn't what AI is for.”

Drayer said it would be better to hire people like herself or other art students to create artwork. She said it would likely leave a better impression especially on younger people against the use of AI.

“A lot of companies and brands everywhere are using AI to make their logos, advertisements, anything like that,” Drayer said. I just hope that in the future it's still a possibility for actual artists to be able to make these logos and brands and that kind of stuff because that's where they started from and I don't know why they have to use AI to continue.”

Many students hope to see the use of AI lessen overtime, and artists like Drayer and Boyde recommend supporting local artists and hope businesses open opportunities for students.

“I would say at least here in Athens, the easiest thing, put up a flyer that just says, ‘hey, we need someone to make some art for this,’” Boyde said. “Hundreds of art students walk by it every day, and I know all of them would love to have something to put on their resume, put on their CV that they worked with a company, made a single piece of art for them to put up.”
